item.title: They Fought the Battle of Brooklyn, After a Bus Ride From New Jersey
item.description:
It was the night before a re-enactment of the Battle of Brooklyn, but efforts to teleport to the past had already begun.

Men shed their modern-day clothes and donned leather neck stocks, gaitered trousers and sleeved waistcoats with buff facings dyed madder red. Some had tents, while others insisted on wool blankets laid on the ground — a nod, they said, to historical accuracy.

Even so, compromises were made. The campsite was not in Brooklyn, but at the Alpine Scout Camp in New Jersey. And when a bottle of contemporary cider was offered, its cap was painstakingly removed with a bayonet.

But the time for libations was short. Just after dawn, some 300 re-enactors — representing Continental, British and German regiments — would descend on Prospect Park to depict the Revolutionary War’s largest battle, and the first to occur after the signing of the Declaration of Independence.

The nation’s 250th anniversary has been an extended Super Bowl for re-enactors, a moment when their passions intersect with a broader interest in the drama of the country’s founding. They relish educating curious onlookers about the war, its characters and a chapter in history that they feel is flattened in service of national identity.

But it’s a quest for verisimilitude that most animates them.

They comb through old letters, search for paintings from the period and locate vintage uniforms to ensure the historical accuracy of their homemade attire. They spend thousands of dollars on materials for these uniforms, which they often fabricate themselves.

And they share battle scars from recreating famous 15-mile marches from the war. (Do lost toenails count?)

Their pursuit of accuracy seemed laudable, if curious. Then, a few weeks before the battle, Niels Hobbs, a leader and elder statesman for a group that portrays His Majesty’s 40th Regiment of Foot, Second Battalion Light Infantry Company, reached out with a question. By text.

Might I be persuaded to join the 40th, dress in British garb and prepare to invade Brooklyn alongside his company?

A few days later, Mr. Hobbs, 50, who teaches marine biology at the University of Rhode Island, added what seemed like a critical proviso.

“Beards were an extreme anomaly in the period — almost bizarrely,” he said, citing my thick facial hair.

“Are you willing to shave?”

Ben Theis, 53, is one of the lead re-enactment organizers, and the prep work for 250th anniversary events like the Battle of Brooklyn began as long as six years ago.

Hiccups are inevitable: The Brooklyn battle was initially to be held at Old Bethpage Village Restoration on Long Island, but Mr. Theis and his fellow organizers were forced to pivot because a wedding at the venue took precedence.

The inconvenience proved fortuitous. They secured a portion of Prospect Park’s largest green space, the Long Meadow, on Aug. 22. The timing and location were a bit of a holy grail for those dedicated to this “living history” genre — on the actual site of the event just five days shy of the battle’s 250th anniversary.

Months earlier, Mr. Theis toured the park on a frigid February day with other event organizers.

His mind raced as he surveyed the expanse and contemplated how the re-enactors would render the grandness of this battle, which originally involved about 30,000 combatants, in one contained corner of the park.

Every re-enactment involves a balance, Mr. Theis observed.

“Eighty percent of it is for the public, and 20 percent of it is for the re-enactors,” he said. “So there are some things that are going to happen that the public may not even see. And that is OK. Think of it as building up the tension.”

In a rowhouse in Philadelphia’s Fishtown neighborhood, Dan Center, a 33-year-old high school history teacher, has his own way of adding to the drama. As a re-enactor for the British, Mr. Center helps tailor kits for his unit, which has roughly 30 active members.

He previously worked at museums, including the Museum of the American Revolution in Philadelphia, and recalled, about a decade ago, portraying a Continental soldier at the Battle of Princeton.

Just as Gen. George Washington’s army had done in January 1777, Mr. Center marched about 14 miles in the cold to Princeton carrying 60 to 80 pounds of gear. The water in his canteen froze, along with the sweat that pooled under his uniform.

Mr. Center was enraptured despite the miserable conditions.

He recalled thinking: “Am I dreaming? Am I actually in a living history event or am I in 1777?”

Each uniform takes Mr. Center between 30 and 40 hours to complete, depending on the rank. The fabrics come from a mill in England that produces the material as it would have been made more than two centuries ago.

Mr. Center’s grandfather served as a tailor in the U.S. Army during World War II, and his great-grandfather made uniforms in the Russian military.

“I actually became a tailor through this hobby,” he said, a musket resting against a nearby wall, a bayonet sitting on the counter beside his blender.

He rattled off other members of his unit who fill critical tasks: shoemakers, tinsmiths, blacksmiths who “make all of the metallurgy and the tools that we use.” There was even “a guy who brews beer the same way it was brewed back then.”

Mr. Center, it turned out, had one more uniform to prepare. I gave him my measurements.

On the eve of battle, the campground in Alpine was filled with re-enactors from as far away as the Carolinas and Quebec portraying British, German and Continental soldiers. They set up tents and stoked fires to cook around.

There would be little of that for Mr. Center, his crew and me.

Light infantry units like the 40th rarely used tents, instead opting for wigwams if it rained or snowed. Mr. Center and Mr. Hobbs outfitted me with a wool blanket, which would be my mattress for the night, along with a uniform, a leather helmet, a musket, a bayonet and an ammo box.

As we prepared our site, another member of the 40th, Daniel Sieh, 32, looked askance at a group of Lexington Minutemen, who laughed as they drank beers and cooked steaks over an open fire.

“My biggest vendetta is against the camp kitchen,” Mr. Sieh said. “All these pots and pans,” he added. “They were not carrying this stuff.”

Mr. Sieh had brought along homemade ship’s biscuits, a rock-hard concoction of flour and water carried by Revolutionary War-era soldiers. He did not bring along his leftovers from dinner at a diner in nearby Northvale, N.J. (He ordered a Reuben sandwich and French fries; I had the Greek salad).

As the evening progressed, acquaintances from other units — both Continental and British — wandered over, to drink beer and cider and smoke clay pipes. They reminisced about past re-enactments and talking excitedly about future ones.

The camaraderie captured the essence of what makes these guys do this, over and over again. It’s not for the money; most of these events, aside from those sponsored by a school or some other institution, involves no pay.

As our fire crackled, I listened as Mr. Hobbs and others noted how they no longer had to wear bellyboxes, cartridge holders worn across a soldier’s stomach. It was a relief to now be portraying a stage in the war when their unit had dispensed with the cumbersome appendage.

“I love the evolution of the British uniform,” Mr. Sieh said. “There is still some pomp and circumstance. But it’s just shaped into a perfect blend of style but also lethality.”

After a fitful night of sleep, we packed up our gear: The Hudson was to be crossed, but by tour buses, with ads for a personal injury lawyer emblazoned on the side.

Upon arriving, we streamed out at Prospect Park West and Third Street in Brooklyn and fell into formation, blending in (but not really) with perplexed residents that included some wearing medals from a half marathon.

As we marched into the park, it became obvious that Mr. Theis’s carefully laid plans might need alterations. Two cannons and a redoubt awaited us in a wooded area, but we couldn’t reach them: Parks workers did not want regiments of redcoats crossing the half-marathon course.

Mr. Hobbs, Mr. Theis and others improvised. We paraded around the Long Meadow, our bayonets attached to our muskets. Thousands of spectators cheered, snapping photos and peppering us redcoats with playful barbs about how we may have won this battle but would (spoiler alert) lose the war.

Then the engagement began. In order to surround the Continental Army, our unit took position on the British right flank, navigating around several women setting up a volleyball net.

The exchange of gunfire began, drawing cheers from the crowd.

Crouched behind Mr. Center in the middle of the Long Meadow, I aimed my musket over his shoulder. Gunpowder stung my eyes. A leather neck stock chafed at my sweat-drenched skin. My feet, coddled from years of proper arch support, throbbed inside reproductions of 18th-century footwear.

Mr. Hobbs, kneeling several yards away, shouted at us to move to higher ground.

“Come on, guards, push them,” Mr. Hobbs yelled at another group of British re-enactors who were supposed to capture Continental regiments.

“We might have to just take them ourselves.”

After the Continental Army’s surrender, the event culminated with a march down Third Street, a route I normally jog. Now I was holding a musket, preening for cheering onlookers in Park Slope as military drummers and fifers played around me. For whatever ambivalence that might exist about this complicated history, the crowd seemed to be having a blast. I was, too.

Our journey ended at the Old Stone House, a recreation of a 17th-century Dutch farmhouse that was nearby and the site of the battle’s climax on Aug. 27, 1776.

There, a Maryland regiment made a last stand that served as a diversion so that the rest of the Continental Army, which was outflanked and outnumbered, could retreat. If General Washington had been captured, the war might have been lost.

Many members of this regiment, who came to be known as the Maryland 400, ended up surrendering to the British, where the Long Meadow is today.

As he milled about afterward, Mr. Theis suggested that the event had ended up being a better spectacle for the public, evincing some disappointment about how much of the re-enactment seemed too far removed from what happened 250 years ago.

He did take some solace in being on the site of the real battle. “This is the spot,” he said. “That is something that we, as re-enactors, we cherish.”

Rather than staying for boxed lunches and a ceremony at the Old Stone House, a cadre of redcoats headed for a nearby bar.

A man posing as Gen. Henry Clinton — a top British commander — sat drinking a Narragansett, frustrated by how disorganized the outing seemed. A sword dangled at his side, and he said that after taking Mounjaro, a GLP-1, he had lost so much weight that he had to fashion a new uniform.

I was somewhat surprised to find my compatriots underwhelmed after a morning that had left me so enthralled.

Mr. Center, Mr. Sieh and Mr. Hobbs were more sanguine, happy to have shown me the ropes and hopeful I’d attend the Battle of White Plains re-enactment in October. More members of the 40th would show, they said, and Mr. Sieh would make one of his famous stews.

That would be the real thing.

The next day Mr. Hobbs graciously texted to see how I felt. My feet were sore, I said, but man, what an experience.

“Yup. Feel all those things,” he replied. “We’re all back home and catching up with modernity. So it goes.”

Julie Snyder contributed reporting.

item.title: My Friend Pocketed the Money From Our Charity Event. What Should I Do?
item.description:
More than a year ago, a friend and I were part of a small organization at our college that occasionally hosted social events, including an annual gathering that was partly an excuse to throw a big party but was also held to raise money for charity. That year, we chose a charity that seemed particularly relevant in the current political climate and would directly help people in our local community.

Leading up to the event, we went all out. My friend took the lead on creating wonderful things for us to sell (in addition to regular donations), and we advertised heavily about the charity we were fund-raising for, which energized everyone to contribute more because of how relevant it felt. All in all, we raised more money than ever. Because we were a small volunteer group, though, we did not have a centralized bank account; we trusted my friend to donate the money after the fact.

He never did. It has now been more than a year, and both he and I and every other leader in that group have graduated and moved away. I did not want to press the issue while he was undergoing a big life shift, so I was willing to allow him to pocket the money temporarily with the promise of donating it later. I don’t think he has gotten a job yet, and I think he is extremely depressed, as he has been ghosting me for the last year.

I feel guilty for keeping this secret, and I don’t know what to do. On one hand, I am trying to show empathy for my friend, who is going through what seems like a very hard time. At the university, the institutional memory is short — most people who remembered the event will be gone soon, if they aren’t already. On the other hand, I feel that we misled everyone. I’m sure people still would have bought what we were selling, but I think the charity part increased sales and donations. The cause is as relevant as ever, and I think what we raised could still make an impact.

What do I owe my friend and what do I owe everyone who donated? Should I, being fortunate enough to have a well-paying job, suck it up and donate the amount myself? Should I let the friendship die, knowing that he essentially stole from a charitable cause? — Name Withheld

From the Ethicist:

Your compassion for your friend is admirable, but personal misery isn’t an excuse for robbing a charity. Nor should you continue to conceal his misconduct in order to preserve your friendship. This man hasn’t just failed to pay up; he has betrayed everyone who organized the event and trusted him to send the money on, and he has let down everyone who bought something or donated, as well as the cause you were all supporting. By the same token, when you say you were “willing to allow him to pocket the money temporarily,” you were implicating yourself in this violation of trust. It wasn’t your call to decide that the charity could be deprived of what it was owed, for however long. You’re entitled to be magnanimous and forgiving about money owed to you. You’re not entitled to be magnanimous and forgiving about money meant for a third party.

Tell your former organization what you know, and make sure that whoever runs it now understands it shouldn’t hold a charity event without a real bank account and real accountability. Write to your friend and tell him you expect him to make the donation immediately. If he can’t, he needs to tell you that. And if he keeps ghosting you, refusing to make this right or even to engage with you about it? Then he’s the one ending the friendship, not you.

You could go on to report what he did to the authorities, but as you appreciate, that’s a grave step. If you’re inclined to go that way, consult your group’s leaders and let them make that call, rather than deciding alone.

Finally, there’s your idea of covering the donation yourself. From what you say, it sounds as if you’re doing well enough, and the sum is small enough, that it wouldn’t be a very great burden. Given that you did keep this secret, wrongly condoning a year of nonpayment, I wouldn’t dismiss the idea. For one thing, it’s the only action you can take that’s guaranteed to cover the charity’s loss. If you do choose to do this, tell your friend what you did and why, and leave it to him whether he ever makes it right.

The previous question was from a stepmother who wondered how to divide up her will. She wrote:

I married my husband more than 50 years ago, when his three children were young. … The children stayed with their mother until the youngest moved in with us at 12. Years later, the eldest, then a graduate student, lived with us for two years. We saw the middle child mostly at family gatherings. … My husband was devoted to family. … He spent much time with his oldest child’s children who lived nearby, and he visited his youngest child’s children, who lived in a neighboring town. But we rarely saw his middle son’s family. … When my husband died five years ago, I inherited the house and bank account. I also own a small condominium. His other substantial financial assets were divided equally among his three children. My will leaves the house to his youngest child, who hopes to live there, and the condo to his eldest and his spouse, who maintain it. The middle child believes both properties should be sold after my death and the proceeds divided equally among the three children. … Should I change my will and divide the property equally among my three stepchildren? — Name Withheld

In his response, the Ethicist noted:

He left the house to you. It’s yours. How your real estate was paid for makes no difference. If you came to think that your husband treated your middle stepchild badly, this judgment might affect how you choose to divide your own estate. To the extent that you had planned to leave him less simply because you thought he had failed in his filial duties, you could certainly recalibrate as you see fit. But you’re not obliged to set things right between the living and the dead. Your closest relationships appear to be with his siblings and their families, not with him and his. It’s entirely reasonable for your will to reflect that reality.

(Reread the full question and answer here.)

⬥

Leaving an unequal inheritance may create problems for your stepchildren’s sibling relationships. It further cements an outsider status. Consider being generous, and let everyone know that is your plan. Perhaps there is a way to reconcile with the middle child. The high road is seldom a bad choice. — Janet

⬥

You can’t right emotional wrongs with money, let alone other people’s. The middle child got an even split of the actual money. That was fair. Leaving your property to those you have a relationship with is also fair. — N.S.H.

⬥

When her husband died, his “substantial” assets were divided equally among his children. That’s that. Dad took care of his kids. He left his wife with the rest, and it is hers to do with as she wishes. She has absolutely no obligation to her stepchildren. — Robert

⬥

I don’t disagree with the counsel provided in the column, but one aspect of the situation seems missing: input from the other siblings. They might have useful things to contribute. — John

⬥

The letter writer has a unique opportunity to heal a deep wound. She did not cause it, and neither the middle child nor his wife sought her intervention, but she’s aware of it now and has the salve in her hands. This is a family she married into, and all the siblings are part of that family. What a powerful way to make a lasting change when she passes. It costs her nothing. — Sardalla

item.title: Should Conservative StudentsAvoid Liberal Colleges?
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Go Ahead, Sean Duffy. Let Your Daughter Go to Harvard,” by David French (column, Aug. 25):

In reassuring conservative parents that sending their children to Harvard will benefit rather than corrupt them, Mr. French — correctly, in our view — dismisses the notion that elite universities sometimes attempt to indoctrinate their students.

Less persuasive is his contention that elite institutions “are often extraordinarily intolerant of dissenting views” and that “peers and professors do sometimes make life difficult for conservative students.”

According to a 2024 Harvard Crimson survey, 76 percent of conservative students feel they belong at Harvard, almost equal to the 79 percent of liberal students who feel the same way. Similar majorities feel respected and connected to their peers. More conservative than liberal students say their goals at Harvard are being met and their well-being is supported.

To be sure, conservative students are less likely than liberals to say they can be their “authentic self” at Harvard, and only 46 percent of conservative students feel comfortable expressing their opinions to others, compared with 75 percent of liberals.

The environment at other elite universities is similar. As a recent Yale report noted, many conservative students find “a real home at Yale,” while also saying their perspectives in some classrooms and communities were “not welcomed or respected.”

Harvard, Yale and other top universities are working, as they should, to address these issues. In the meantime, concerned parents — and the public — should look at the facts, not conservative talking points.

David WippmanGlenn AltschulerThe writers are, respectively, a president emeritus of Hamilton College and a professor emeritus of American studies at Cornell University.

To the Editor:

The “left-wing monoculture” that David French writes about is not a monolith. Ideological echo chambers can be pried open by anyone who can recognize a teachable moment and is willing to speak out.

During the 2006 midterms, whose environment has been compared to that of this year’s elections, I was teaching at a college where most students were strongly left of center. The day after the election, I walked into my Latin class to find my students boisterous with delight over the Republican defeat. I read them the riot act.

“What are you doing?” I said. “What if there are students in here who are sorry that the Republicans lost? Now they’re not only sorry about their candidates, but they also feel like no one cares.”

A sheepish hush fell over the room. There were several chastened mumblings of “sorry, Professor.” Lesson learned, or so I thought, but it turned out the lesson went even further than I had realized. Later one of the students approached me. “Thank you for saying that,” he said quietly. “That student was me.”

Deborah BeckAustin, Texas

To the Editor:

David French writes of his experience being a conservative and a Christian at Harvard Law School. Mr. French believes that the law school was a liberal bubble, but he appreciated his time being a distinct religious and ideological minority. He says he appreciated “being tested by the smartest people I had ever met” and that, as a result, he is now “a better conservative because they tested me.”

My own experience at Harvard Law School was rather different from Mr. French’s. I entered in 1987 after a career in radical left-wing politics. (I was the only felon in my law school graduating class, having burglarized 14 draft boards during the Vietnam War.) But Harvard Law School was not a liberal bubble.

A majority of my first-year professors were well-known conservatives. One had been an assistant attorney general in the Justice Department under President Ronald Reagan. Another was a prominent anti-abortion lawyer.

During my time at Harvard, two progressive legal scholars — David Trubek and Clare Dalton — were denied tenure at the law school. I, like many others, believed that this was because of their politics, not their scholarship.

While I heartily disagree with Mr. French about Harvard Law School being part of a liberal bubble, I just as heartily agree with him that I appreciated having my philosophical, political and ethical beliefs challenged by the smartest people I had ever met. I am a better progressive because they tested me.

Jerry ElmerProvidence, R.I.

To the Editor:

The common conservative idea that kids can be ruined by attending universities that are known to be more liberal is just parochial paranoia. The idea that no one should ever change his or her mind about any number of issues or ideas shows the weakness of conservative thought. The most important lesson that liberal institutions impart to students is the ability to defend their positions and the clarity to see when ideas have no validity.

I also grew up in a conservative culture with strong religious underpinnings. When I left for the most liberal college in the state, my parents worried. But after several years they announced that my vocabulary was much broader and my interests were more varied, and my 50-year-old mother enrolled as a freshman at that school.

Fear of the unknown shouldn’t choke your child’s development.

Shari ReedAlbuquerque

To the Editor:

David French’s column about conservatives at liberal colleges would have been much improved if he had included experiences of liberal students at conservative colleges.

Would they have similar reports of being shouted down in class and having difficult conversations with their parents? I suspect so.

Cecilia CordeiroCambridge, Mass.
